items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: Clarence Williams came to the hotel where I live with a letter of introduction by Mr. Pierron, who I had corresponded with.

ctx.x: Well you mentioned Pierron's band and what type of music they play. I forgot to mention it was in the year about 1915. I think Pierron then used mostly string instruments. And he played regular conventional ragtime like I had right on records that was of that date of error. There's some things I'd like to tell you that I may have forgotten to mention. items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: Clarence Williams would only be 13 years of age. He was still in the country, in Plaquemine, Louisiana.

ctx.x: Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his…

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13.…

items.q: The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron

ctx.x: Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just…

items.q: it was royal garden blues for spencer and clarence

ctx.x: it's quite a popular belief i believe that the original dixieland jazz band and you in particular discriminated against the colored people if that is so perhaps some of these people who think themselves so clever and these people who have all the say so in the books and magazines and so on would care to reflect on the number of tunes recorded and played by the original dixieland jazz band that were written by colored men that doesn't look like the discrimination to me think of them there's mammy oh mine by maceo…

discrimination to me and not only that i played saint louis blues for handy oh yes of course i was forgetting that and our picture was on all these colored publications it was royal garden blues for spencer and clarence that's right spencer claren williams our pictures was on all their publications they were willing to ride our back to get up now that they got up there they tried to bury me but there's two lane archers opened up and i hope to see the future historians and scholars look into the truth and see…

thing before i close that there are recordings made at the same time as yours around 1921 by colored people of numbers like royal garden blues and jasmine blues and i listened to them and they do not contain anything like the same spirit of jazz as yours do they're obviously they're stodgy they're obviously striving after it they're the first attempts to follow and they're trying very hard perhaps they're trying too hard but they don't get there they don't flow they don't move they don't excite the dance anyone…
